draft.title: Ohm's law
card: Voltage is the energy given to each unit of charge, measured in volts (V). Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance is how much a part opposes the current, measured in ohms (Ω).
Ohm's law links the three: V = I × R. Voltage equals current times resistance.
If the resistance stays fixed, more voltage gives more current. Doubling the voltage doubles the current.
The law can be rearranged to find current, I = V ÷ R, or resistance, R = V ÷ I. For example, 12 V across a 4 Ω resistor gives a current of 3 A.
draft.remember: V = IR. With a fixed resistance, current rises as voltage rises.

a.q: A resistor has a fixed resistance. The voltage across it is doubled. What happens to the current through it?
a.why: With R fixed, I = V ÷ R, so current is in proportion to voltage. Doubling the voltage doubles the current. It does not halve, because a higher voltage pushes more charge through, not less.
a.clue: Resistance stays fixed, so current follows voltage.

b.q: A heater element in Tom's workshop has a resistance of 40 Ω. It is connected to a 240 V supply. What current flows through it?
b.why: I = V ÷ R = 240 ÷ 40 = 6 A. Multiplying the two numbers gives 9600, which is the common mistake. Current is found by dividing voltage by resistance.
b.clue: To find current, divide voltage by resistance.
